action_criteria.label: Core laboratory work-up: blood count, electrolytes, renal and liver function, glucose, INR, ammonia and CRP, with toxicology where alcohol or drugs are in question; urinalysis for the urinary symptoms
action_criteria.rationale: Confirms liver dysfunction and identifies metabolic and infective precipitants; here also the severity of sepsis and the kidney injury [ACG_HE_2026]

action_criteria.rationale: Fever 38.6 °C with leucocytosis and a urinary source: blood cultures are drawn before the first antibiotic dose [EASL_HE_2022]

action_criteria.label: Diagnostic paracentesis: cell count with differential, total protein and albumin, Gram stain and culture in blood-culture bottles
action_criteria.rationale: Every hospitalised patient with cirrhosis, ascites and encephalopathy needs a diagnostic paracentesis to exclude SBP, here even though a urinary source is evident

action_criteria.rationale: Right loin pain, kidney injury and an E. coli urinary infection: obstruction or a renal or perinephric collection must be excluded because either needs drainage, and kidney injury in cirrhosis calls for renal ultrasound [EASL_decomp_2018]

action_criteria.rationale: In hepatitis B cirrhosis that decompensates on treatment, the viral load separates a flare or virological breakthrough from another precipitant and decides whether adherence or the antiviral needs review [EASL_HBV_2025]

action_criteria.rationale: Kidney injury changes the tenofovir dose and the safety of her diuretics and beta-blocker, and the sulfonamide allergy excludes co-trimoxazole for the SBP prophylaxis she will need [EASL_decomp_2018]

prohibited_recommendations: Do not give benzodiazepines or other sedatives for agitation or sleep: they precipitate and prolong hepatic encephalopathy; manage agitation with reorientation, a safe environment and treatment of the precipitant (EASL 2022).
Do not prescribe sedating opioids, which worsen hepatic encephalopathy; use acetaminophen up to 2 g per day for pain.
Do not stop HBV antiviral therapy during acute illness (flare risk).
Do not use co-trimoxazole for treatment or prophylaxis: documented sulfonamide antibiotic allergy.
Avoid nephrotoxic drugs (NSAIDs, aminoglycosides, IV contrast where avoidable) during the kidney injury.
required_recommendations: Sepsis care: cultures then IV antibiotic within one hour, volume with albumin, monitor lactate, urine output and creatinine, ICU review if hypotension persists (EASL 2018).

Treat the E. coli pyelonephritis with IV ceftriaxone 2 g daily after cultures, adjusted to the susceptibilities (ceftriaxone-susceptible), for 10-14 days with oral step-down once stable; drain any obstruction or collection the ultrasound shows.
Blood, urine and ascitic cultures are drawn before the first antibiotic dose, which is not delayed for them.

Kidney injury (creatinine 1.8 mg/dL): stop spironolactone, furosemide and propranolol, give IV albumin 1 g/kg (up to 100 g) per day for two days, replace potassium to 4.0 mEq/L or more, because hypokalemia increases renal ammoniagenesis, and monitor creatinine and urine output (EASL 2018).

Lactulose 25 mL every 1-2 hours until at least two soft bowel movements, then titrated to 2-3 soft bowel movements per day (ACG 2026 recommendation 10; EASL 2022); avoid over-titration, which causes dehydration, hypokalemia and kidney injury. Continue rifaximin 550 mg twice daily.

Continue hepatitis B antiviral therapy without interruption, adjusted to the creatinine clearance (tenofovir disoproxil every 48 hours at 30-49 mL/min) or switched to tenofovir alafenamide or entecavir; HBV DNA 340 IU/mL on treatment: check adherence and repeat HBV DNA (EASL 2025 hepatitis B guideline).

After the acute course, give primary SBP prophylaxis (ascitic protein 0.9 g/dL with bilirubin 9.8 mg/dL and creatinine 1.8 mg/dL) with ciprofloxacin, not co-trimoxazole (sulfonamide allergy) (EASL 2018; AASLD 2021).
Stop omeprazole unless there is a specific indication: proton pump inhibitors are associated with SBP and HE in cirrhosis (EASL 2022).
Refer for liver transplant assessment: decompensated cirrhosis with overt HE, MELD-Na 32, and a single 1.8 cm hepatocellular carcinoma within the Milan criteria (EASL 2018).

avoided_actions.rationale: No clinical suspicion for hepatopulmonary syndrome, portopulmonary hypertension, or endocarditis; echocardiography is not part of the HE workup.
Amyloid PET has no role in HE workup; reversible metabolic encephalopathy is the issue, not Alzheimer pathology.
DaTscan has no role in HE workup; the question is metabolic encephalopathy, not nigrostriatal degeneration.
Early-onset AD genetic panel has no role in HE workup; reversible metabolic encephalopathy is the diagnosis under consideration.

accepted: Hepatic encephalopathy (West Haven grade III), hepatitis B cirrhosis (Child-Pugh C, MELD-Na 32), precipitated by E. coli urosepsis (right pyelonephritis); ascites mandates SBP exclusion.

differential.key_features: Ascites in an infected cirrhotic makes a tap mandatory regardless of the urinary source; the ascitic PMN of 162 cells/mm3 (below 250) with a sterile culture excludes SBP.

differential.diagnosis: Sepsis-associated encephalopathy as the sole cause
differential.key_features: E. coli pyelonephritis with fever 38.6 °C, HR 114, lactate 2.9 mmol/L and kidney injury contributes; blood cultures are sterile; asterixis and decompensated liver disease point to HE precipitated by the sepsis, and the two coexist.
HBV DNA 340 IU/mL on tenofovir is low-level viremia (adherence or renal dosing to review), not a flare: ALT 118 U/L, HBeAg negative; tenofovir is continued.
Abstinent for 2 years; blood ethanol not detected.
Right loin pain, fever and kidney injury raise it; the ultrasound shows no hydronephrosis and no renal or perinephric collection.

key_clinical_evidence: HE is a clinical diagnosis: West Haven grade, evidence of liver disease and exclusion of other causes of altered mental status (ACG 2026; EASL 2022).

Precipitant identification is more actionable than the ammonia number: infection (SBP especially), GI bleed, electrolyte disturbance (hypokalemia/hyponatremia), constipation, sedative/CNS-depressant use, dehydration, dietary protein load, renal failure.
HBV cirrhotics on suppressive antivirals should not have therapy interrupted during acute illness.
Child-Pugh C (15: bilirubin 9.8 3, albumin 2.2 3, INR 2.4 3, moderate ascites 3, HE grade 3 3); MELD-Na 32 (creatinine 1.8, bilirubin 9.8, INR 2.4, sodium 131)

An elevated ammonia neither grades nor confirms hepatic encephalopathy and repeat levels are not used to guide treatment; a normal ammonia in a confused patient with cirrhosis should prompt a search for another cause (ACG 2026 recommendation 5 and key concept 14; EASL 2022).
Loin pain with fever and kidney injury in a urinary infection calls for renal imaging: an obstructed or abscessed kidney needs drainage, not antibiotics alone.

patient.history_present_illness: Ms. T. is a 55-year-old Black woman with hepatitis B cirrhosis (Child-Pugh B at her last clinic review) and prior hepatic encephalopathy who was brought to the emergency department by her daughter for worsening confusion over the past 36 hours. The daughter arrived for her daily check and found her mother disoriented — she could not remember the current year and was confused about her location. The daughter also noted her mother had been complaining of pain with urination and lower abdominal pain for 5 days but had self-medicated with cranberry juice and refused to call her doctor. On arrival the patient has a temperature of 38.6°C, heart rate 114, and blood pressure 106/62. Right lower quadrant tenderness and right loin pain are present. Ascites is present on exam.

neurological_exam.additional: Scleral icterus. Mild jaundice. Moderate ascites. Spider angiomata on upper chest. Fetor hepaticus. Temperature 38.6°C. No meningism. Right lower quadrant tenderness on deep palpation. Right loin pain.
